:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
The substitution $z=y^m$ for some real number $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + x^3y= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{y}}
$$

into an equation of the form $z'(x) + P(x)z(x) = Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x) = x^3, \qquad q(x) = 1, \qquad n=-\dfrac12.
$$

First, we multiply the differential equation by $y^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
y^{1/2} \dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + x^3y^{3/2}= 1.\qquad\qquad (\ast)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z= y^{1-n} =  y^{3/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = \dfrac{3}{2}y^{1/2} \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y^{1/2}\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{2}{3}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(\ast)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{2}{3}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + x^3\,z = 1
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{3}{2}x^3z = \dfrac{3}{2}.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x) = \dfrac{3}{2}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}y=x{y}^{4}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={x}^{2},\,q(x)=x,\,n=4.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{4},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-4}\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}{y}^{-3}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-3}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-3{y}^{-4}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-4}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}z=x
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-3{x}^{2}z=-3x.
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=-3{x}^{2}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some real number $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x}=x\sqrt{y}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,q(x)=x,\,n=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-1/2}\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{{y}^{1/2}}{x}=x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-1/2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
2\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}\,z=x
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{2x}\,z=\frac{x}{2}.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)=\frac{x}{2}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}-y(2x+3{y}^{2})=0
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}-y(2x+3{y}^{2}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}-2xy-3{y}^{3} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}-2xy & =3{y}^{3} \\ \frac{dy}{dx}-2{x}^{-1}y & =3{x}^{-2}{y}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-2{x}^{-1},\,q(x)=3{x}^{-2},\,n=3.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3}\frac{dy}{dx}-2{x}^{-1}{y}^{-2}=3{x}^{-2}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-2{y}^{-3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-2{x}^{-1}z=3{x}^{-2}
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+4{x}^{-1}z=-6{x}^{-2}.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)=-6{x}^{-2}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some real number $m$ transform the differential equation

$$
{y}^{1/2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}{y}^{3/2}-y=0
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rearrange the equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{1/2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}{y}^{3/2}-y & =0 \\ {y}^{1/2}\,\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}{y}^{3/2} & =y \\ \frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}y & ={y}^{1/2}\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={x}^{2},\,q(x)=1,\,n=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Now, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-1/2}\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}{y}^{1/2}=1.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}{y}^{-1/2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-1/2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=2\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
2\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}z=1
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}\,z=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-y\operatorname{tan}⁡x={y}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-\operatorname{tan}⁡x,\,q(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,n=5.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{5},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-5}\frac{dy}{dx}-{y}^{-4}\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-4}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-4{y}^{-5}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-5}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{4}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{4}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z\operatorname{tan}⁡x=\operatorname{cos}⁡x
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+4z\operatorname{tan}⁡x=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)=-4\operatorname{cos}⁡x$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+3xy=-{x}^{4}{y}^{3}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=3x,\,q(x)=-{x}^{4},\,n=3.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3}\frac{dy}{dx}+3x{y}^{-2}=-{x}^{4}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-2{y}^{-3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+3xz=-{x}^{4}
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-6xz=2{x}^{4}.
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=-6x.$

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{y}{x}={x}^{3}{y}^{3/4}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=\frac{1}{x},\,q(x)={x}^{3},\,n=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{3/4},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-3/4}\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{{y}^{1/4}}{x}={x}^{3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{1/4}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}{y}^{-3/4}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-3/4}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=4\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
4\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{x}\,z={x}^{3}
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{1}{4x}\,z=\frac{{x}^{3}}{4}.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)=\frac{{x}^{3}}{4}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some real number $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}y=\frac{{x}^{3}}{\sqrt{y}}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)={x}^{2},\,q(x)={x}^{3},\,n=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

First, we multiply the differential equation by ${y}^{1/2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{1/2}\frac{dy}{dx}+{x}^{2}{y}^{3/2}={x}^{3}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{3/2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{2}{y}^{1/2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{1/2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+{x}^{2}\,z={x}^{3}
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}\,z=\frac{3{x}^{3}}{2}.
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=\frac{3{x}^{2}}{2}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some integer $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+y=-\frac{x}{y}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $Q(x)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=1,\,q(x)=-x,\,n=-1.
$$

First, we multiply the differential equation by $y,$ and we get

$$
y\frac{dy}{dx}+{y}^{2}=-x.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2y\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-x
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2z=-2x.
$$

Therefore, $Q(x)=-2x.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
The substitution $z={y}^{m}$ for some real number $m$ transforms the differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}-xy=\frac{\sqrt[3]{y}}{{x}^{5}}
$$

into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)+P(x)z(x)=Q(x).$ What is the function $P(x)?$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-x,\,q(x)={x}^{-5},\,n=\frac{1}{3}.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{1/3},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-1/3}\frac{dy}{dx}-x{y}^{2/3}=\frac{1}{{x}^{5}}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{2/3}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{3}{y}^{-1/3}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-1/3}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, equation $(∗)$ can be written as a linear equation in $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\frac{3}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-x\,z=\frac{1}{{x}^{5}}
$$

Finally, we write the above equation in standard form, which gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{2x}{3}\,z=\frac{2}{3{x}^{5}}.
$$

Therefore, $P(x)=-\frac{2x}{3}.$
